mortality was observed in the 12-year mortality follow-up of the Canada Fitness Survey (Katzmarzyk et al., 2009). At baseline,
sitting time was classiﬁed into 5 groups: almost none of the time, one-fourth of the time, half of the time, three-fourths of the
time, and almost all of the time. After adjustment for potential confounders, there was a higher risk of all-cause mortality (HRs:
1.00, 1.00, 1.11, 1.36, 1.54; P for trend <0.0001) and CVD mortality (HR: 1.00, 1.01, 1.22, 1.47, 1.54; P for trend <0.0001) across
successively higher levels of sitting time (Katzmarzyk et al., 2009). The following year, similar results were obtained in a 6.6-year
follow-up of the Australian Diabetes, Obesity and Lifestyle Study (AusDiab), where there was a signiﬁcant positive association
between television viewing time and mortality from all-causes and from CVD (Dunstan et al., 2010). After adjustment for covari-
ates, the HRs for each 1 h increment in daily television viewing time were 1.11 (95% CI: 1.03 to 1.20) for all-cause mortality and
1.18 (95% CI: 1.03 to 1.35) for CVD mortality (Dunstan et al., 2010).
